result:
The proposed answer of 1/10 is correct, though the boundary argument is sketched loosely.

**Graph structure.** For $a<b$, the vertex $\{a,b\}$ is adjacent to $\{a\pm1,b\}$ when the new pair stays in the region, and to $\{a,b\pm1\}$ likewise. So $T_2(P_n)$ is exactly the induced subgraph of the integer grid on $R=\{(a,b):1\le a<b\le n\}$, with $|R|=\binom n2$.

**Perfect code.** $S=\{(x,y): 2x+y\equiv 0 \pmod 5\}$ is a perfect dominating set of $\mathbb{Z}^2$. The closed neighborhood of a vertex with residue $r$ has residues $r, r\pm1, r\pm2$, which covers all five classes, so each vertex has exactly one dominator in $S$.

**Lower bound.** A vertex dominates at most 5 vertices, so $\gamma\ge |R|/5=\tfrac15\binom n2$.

**Upper bound.** Take $S\cap R$. The only vertices of $R$ left undominated are those whose unique $S$-dominator lies outside $R$. These lie within distance 1 of the boundary of the triangle, which has $O(n)$ vertices, so adding $O(n)$ extra vertices fixes them. Hence $\gamma\le \tfrac15\binom n2+O(n)$.

**Limit.** $\gamma(T_2(P_n))=\frac{n(n-1)}{10}+O(n)$, so $\dfrac{\gamma}{n^2}\to\dfrac1{10}$.

**Small case.** For $n=4$, the vertex $(1,3)$ and then $(2,4)$ dominate all six vertices, and one vertex cannot suffice, so $\gamma=2$, which matches the claim.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
CONFIDENCE: 4
